Fitting jump distance (JD) data

Source: R/fittingJD.R
fittingJD.Rd

Jump Distances have been calculated for a given time lag. They can be described by fitting curves to the data, either using a histogram or cumulative probability density function. Firtting to a histogram is sensitive to binning parameters and ECDF performs better for general use. The idea behind this analysis is given in: - Weimann et al. (2013) A quantitative comparison of single-dye tracking analysis tools using Monte Carlo simulations. PloS One 8, e64287. - Menssen & Mani (2019) A Jump-Distance-Based Parameter Inference Scheme for Particulate Trajectories, Biophysical Journal, 117: 1, 143-156. This function is called from inside `makeSummaryReport()`, using the defaults. However, you can pass additional arguments for `nPop`, `init` and `breaks` via the ellipsis. Fitting is tricky and two populations (default) is written to catch errors and retry. In the case of failure, try passing better guesses via `init`. To fit 3 populations, you must pass `nPop = 3` as an additional argument, you are advised to also pass guesses via `init`.

Usage

fittingJD(jumpList)

Arguments

jumpList

list of a data frame (with a column named jump of jump distances), and a list of params

Value

ggplot

Examples

xmlPath <- system.file("extdata", "ExampleTrackMateData.xml", package="TrackMateR")
tmObj <- readTrackMateXML(XMLpath = xmlPath)
#> Units are:  1 pixel and 0.07002736 s 
#> Spatial units are in pixels - consider transforming to real units
#> Extracting spot data...
#> Matching track data...
#> Calculating distances...
tmObj <- correctTrackMateData(tmObj, xyscalar = 0.04)
#> Correcting XY scale. 
jdObj <- calculateJD(dataList = tmObj, deltaT = 2)
fittingJD(jumpList = jdObj)
